title: Latency vs Throughput
subtitle: Two different speeds — and the numbers that let you reject a bad design in 30 seconds
objectives: Tell latency and throughput apart, and know which fix applies to which
Recall the order-of-magnitude latency numbers and do back-of-envelope math
Reason with percentiles and explain why fan-out turns rare slowness into the norm
Explain how utilization, queueing, and Little's Law connect throughput back to latency

exercises.prompt: Think of a pipe carrying water. Latency is how long one drop takes to travel it; throughput is how much water flows per second. Which change raises throughput but does NOT improve latency?
exercises.why: A wider pipe carries more water per second (throughput), but a single drop still takes exactly as long to travel end to end (latency). Only shortening the pipe cuts latency.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the whole unit in one image. It's also why 'we added more servers but my page is still slow' is such a common and painful surprise — more servers widened the pipe; they didn't shorten it.

exercises.prompt: ______ is the time for one request to complete; throughput is how many complete per second.
exercises.why: Latency = time per operation. Throughput = operations per unit time. They're different axes, and improving one can even hurt the other.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Max data per second the link can carry

exercises.why: Latency is per-request time; throughput is completed work per second; bandwidth is the ceiling the physical link imposes; RTT is the there-and-back time that dominates network latency.
exercises.goDeeper: Bandwidth and throughput get confused constantly. Bandwidth is the pipe's capacity; throughput is what you actually achieve through it. You can have a fat pipe and terrible throughput if something else is the bottleneck.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually reduce LATENCY for a single request? Select all.
choices: Caching the result so the work is already done
Moving the server geographically closer to the user
exercises.why: Latency falls when you shorten the work or the distance: cache it, move closer, make the query faster. Adding servers adds capacity to run more requests at once — it doesn't make any single request's work finish sooner.
exercises.goDeeper: Internalize this split and you'll diagnose faster than most engineers: latency problems are solved by doing less work or travelling less distance; throughput problems are solved by adding parallel capacity. Reaching for the wrong lever is the classic wasted quarter.

exercises.prompt: You double your server count. Users still say each page takes 2 seconds. Why didn't it get faster?
choices: The new servers need a restart
More servers add throughput (capacity to serve more users), not lower per-request latency
Servers always fix latency — something is misconfigured
DNS is caching the old servers
exercises.why: Scaling out lets you handle MORE simultaneous requests. It does nothing to shorten the work inside any one request — so each user still waits 2 seconds.
exercises.goDeeper: Scaling out only helps a user's latency indirectly: if servers were overloaded and queueing, adding capacity removes the waiting. That's the exception that proves the rule — and it's exactly what the boss lesson of this unit is about.

exercises.prompt: Your API serves 10,000 requests per second, and each one takes 200ms. Which is the throughput?
exercises.why: Throughput is the rate of completed work: 10,000 requests/second. The 200ms is the latency of one request.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice these two numbers coexist happily. A system can be high-throughput AND high-latency at the same time (a huge batch pipeline), or low-throughput and low-latency (a tiny, snappy service).

exercises.prompt: Roughly how much slower is reading from main memory (RAM) than from the CPU's L1 cache?
exercises.why: L1 cache is roughly 1 nanosecond; RAM is roughly 100 nanoseconds. That's about 100× — and RAM is the thing we usually call 'fast.'
exercises.goDeeper: The memory hierarchy is a ladder of ~100× cliffs: cache → RAM → SSD → network → disk seek → cross-continent. Every step down costs orders of magnitude. Knowing roughly where each rung sits is what lets you reason about performance without measuring.

exercises.prompt: Reading from main memory (RAM) takes roughly how many nanoseconds?
exercises.why: A main-memory reference is on the order of 100 nanoseconds. These figures are order-of-magnitude, not precise — the point is the scale, not the digits.
exercises.goDeeper: Compare: L1 cache ≈ 1 ns. So even a RAM hit — which feels instant — is ~100 cache misses' worth of time. This is why cache-friendly data layouts can make code several times faster without changing the algorithm.

exercises.prompt: A network round trip between two servers in the SAME datacenter takes roughly how many microseconds?
exercises.why: A same-datacenter round trip is on the order of 500 microseconds (about half a millisecond). Fast by human standards — enormously slow by CPU standards.
exercises.goDeeper: Note it's already ~5,000× slower than a RAM read, and you haven't even left the building. Leaving the building (cross-continent) costs another ~300×, landing around 150ms.

exercises.prompt: Match each operation to its rough order of magnitude.
exercises.why: The ladder: 1 ns → 100 ns → 100 µs → 150 ms. From cache to a cross-continent hop is roughly 100 million times slower.
exercises.goDeeper: Worth noticing: an SSD read (~100 µs) is FASTER than a same-datacenter network round trip (~500 µs). Reading from your own disk can beat asking a neighbouring server. That inverts a lot of people's intuitions about 'just put it in another service.'

exercises.prompt: A RAM read is ~100ns. A same-datacenter network call is ~0.5ms. Roughly how many RAM reads fit inside ONE network call?
exercises.why: 0.5ms = 500,000ns. Divided by 100ns per RAM read = about 5,000. One 'cheap' internal network hop costs roughly five thousand memory reads.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the number that should haunt every microservice design. Adding one service hop to a request path isn't a rounding error — it's thousands of times more expensive than doing the work locally. Chatty service meshes die of exactly this, one innocent-looking call at a time.

exercises.prompt: Why bother memorizing these order-of-magnitude numbers at all?
choices: To impress people in code review
To do back-of-envelope math and reject a bad design in seconds — without building it
They're required by the HTTP spec
They're only useful for embedded programming
exercises.why: Rough numbers let you kill a bad design with arithmetic instead of a three-month build. 'That's 10,000 serial network calls at 0.5ms — five seconds. No.' That takes 30 seconds and saves a quarter.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the single most transferable skill in system design, and the reason estimation questions show up in every interview. You're not being tested on the digits — you're being tested on whether you can reason about scale before committing to it.

exercises.prompt: Your dashboard says average latency is 100ms — healthy. Users are furious that the app is slow. How can both be true?
choices: The average hides the tail: a small share of requests could be taking 5+ seconds
exercises.why: Averages smear outliers away. If 95% of requests take 50ms and 5% take 2 seconds, the average still looks fine — while 1 in 20 users has a terrible time.
exercises.goDeeper: Average latency is arguably the most misleading metric in all of systems. Nobody experiences the average. Every user experiences one specific request — and the unhappy ones are living in your tail.

exercises.prompt: Match each metric to what it actually tells you.

pairs.right: Half of requests are faster than this
95% are faster; the slowest 5% are worse

exercises.why: Percentiles describe the distribution instead of collapsing it. p50 is the typical experience; p99 is the bad one you promised not to inflict.
exercises.goDeeper: Teams often watch p50 and feel great. Your most valuable users — the ones with the most data, the biggest carts, the longest histories — usually live in the p99. The tail isn't random; it's often systematically your heaviest users.

exercises.prompt: Your p99 latency is 2 seconds. What does that mean?
choices: 99% of requests are faster than 2 seconds; the slowest 1% are worse
exercises.why: p99 = the value 99% of requests come in under. The remaining 1% are slower — and 2s is the floor of their pain, not the ceiling.
exercises.goDeeper: 1% sounds negligible until you multiply. At 10,000 requests/second, that's 100 bad experiences every second — roughly 8.6 million a day. 'Rare' at scale is a full-time disaster.

exercises.prompt: At 10,000 requests/second, how many requests per second land in your p99 tail (the slowest 1%)?
exercises.why: 1% of 10,000 = 100 requests every second hitting your worst-case latency. Percentages feel small; rates feel real.
exercises.goDeeper: Always convert percentages into absolute rates before deciding something is acceptable. '99.9% success' at 10k rps is still 10 failures per second — 864,000 a day.

exercises.prompt: A page makes 100 parallel calls to internal services. Each has p99 = 100ms (so each has a 1% chance of being slow). Roughly what fraction of page loads hit AT LEAST ONE slow call?
exercises.why: Each call is fast 99% of the time. All 100 being fast = 0.99^100 ≈ 37%. So about 63% of page loads hit at least one slow call. A 1-in-100 event becomes the majority experience.
exercises.goDeeper: This is Google's famous 'tail at scale.' When you fan out, your dependencies' p99 becomes your page's p50. It's the mathematical reason microservice architectures feel mysteriously slow — nobody's service is broken, yet the page is always waiting on someone.

exercises.prompt: Which of these genuinely help tame tail latency? Select all.
choices: Hedged requests: send a duplicate and take whichever answers first
exercises.why: Hedging routes around a straggler, timeouts stop one slow dependency from holding the whole page hostage, and less fan-out means fewer chances to draw a slow call. Running at 100% utilization does the opposite — it's a tail-latency generator.
exercises.goDeeper: Hedged requests feel wasteful (you're deliberately duplicating work) but they're a real technique at Google-scale: a few percent extra load can cut p99 dramatically. Trading a little throughput for a lot of tail is often a superb deal.

exercises.prompt: You're writing a latency SLA for your service. Which metric should it be written against?
choices: The average — it's the most representative
A high percentile like p95 or p99 — it bounds the worst experience users actually hit
The minimum — it shows what's possible
The maximum — the absolute worst case
exercises.why: An SLA is a promise about the bad case, not the typical one. Percentiles bound real user pain; averages hide it, and the max is one pathological outlier you can't control.
exercises.goDeeper: The max is usually useless — a single GC pause or network blip owns it forever. p99 (or p99.9 at big scale) is the honest, actionable promise.

exercises.prompt: Your server handles requests comfortably at 50ms when it's half busy. You push it to 99% utilization. What happens to latency?
choices: It stays around 50ms — the work per request didn't change
It drops, because the CPU is warmed up
It explodes: requests queue behind each other, and wait time grows non-linearly
exercises.why: The work per request didn't change, but now requests WAIT. As utilization approaches 100%, queueing delay grows non-linearly — at 99% busy, latency can be tens of times worse than at 50% busy.
exercises.goDeeper: This is queueing theory, and it's the bridge between throughput and latency. Rule of thumb: keep utilization meaningfully below 100% — often around 70%. That 'wasted' headroom is not waste; it's what you're buying low latency with. A server at 100% utilization isn't efficient — it's one hiccup from a meltdown.

exercises.prompt: Little's Law says: concurrency = throughput × latency. Your service handles 500 requests/second, each taking 0.2 seconds. How many requests are in flight at any moment?
exercises.why: 500 requests/sec × 0.2 sec = 100 requests in flight. That's how many are being worked on simultaneously.
exercises.goDeeper: This tiny formula tells you how many threads, connections, or workers you need. And it has teeth: if latency doubles (a dependency slows down), in-flight requests double — with zero change in traffic. That's how you exhaust a connection pool and turn one slow dependency into a full outage.

exercises.prompt: Little's Law again: 200 requests/second, each taking 0.5 seconds. How many requests are in flight?
exercises.why: 200 × 0.5 = 100 in flight. Throughput × latency = concurrency, every time.
exercises.goDeeper: Run it backwards to size a pool: if you want 1,000 rps at 50ms latency, you need 1,000 × 0.05 = 50 concurrent workers. Capacity planning in one multiplication.

exercises.prompt: You batch 100 database writes together instead of writing them one at a time. What happens?
choices: Throughput goes up, but an individual write's latency goes up — it waits for the batch to fill
exercises.why: Batching spreads fixed per-operation costs across many items, so total throughput rises. But each individual write now waits for the batch to assemble — so its own latency gets worse. You trade the individual's speed for the system's capacity.
exercises.goDeeper: This tradeoff is everywhere once you see it: Kafka batching, database group commit, Nagle's algorithm in TCP. It's the purest example that latency and throughput aren't just different — they're often in direct opposition.

exercises.prompt: You're designing 'send message' in a real-time chat app. Slide toward what you'd optimize.
exercises.why: A human is staring at the screen waiting for their message to appear. Latency wins decisively — batching would add delay to the one thing the user is watching.
exercises.goDeeper: The question to always ask: is a human waiting? If yes, optimize latency. If no — logs, analytics, nightly ETL, ingestion pipelines — optimize throughput and batch hard. Same system, opposite answers, decided entirely by who's on the other end.

exercises.prompt: Your pipeline: Load Balancer (10k rps) → App servers (2k rps) → Cache (50k rps) → Database (5k rps). What's the maximum throughput of the whole system?
exercises.why: A chain is limited by its slowest stage — the app servers at 2k rps. Everything downstream is idle capacity you're paying for and can't use.
exercises.goDeeper: The corollary is brutal and constantly ignored: optimizing a NON-bottleneck yields exactly zero improvement. Making the cache twice as fast here changes nothing. Measure first, find the actual constraint, then fix that — anything else is theatre.

exercises.prompt: Users report the site is slow. Average latency looks fine at 80ms. CPU sits at 95%. p99 latency is 4 seconds. Diagnosis?
choices: Nothing's wrong — the average is healthy
The servers are near saturation, so queueing is exploding the tail: most requests are fine, but the p99 is brutal. Add headroom or cut work per request
exercises.why: 95% CPU puts you deep in the queueing danger zone. The average hides it because most requests still sail through — but the ones that arrive during a burst wait behind a queue, and that's your 4-second p99. The fix is headroom (capacity) or less work per request, not a micro-optimization.
exercises.goDeeper: This ties the whole unit together: latency and throughput are different (lesson 1), you need the numbers to reason (lesson 2), averages lie so you watch percentiles (lesson 3), and utilization is the hidden variable connecting them all. High utilization looks like efficiency on a cost dashboard and feels like a broken product to users.
